ChatGPT , are trained to predict the next most likely word that will follow based on the text

LLM is a base LLM to be ﬁne-tuned, using various techniques, including Reinforcement

have improved their ability to align with purpose, overcoming the limitations in the base
model, being safe and less biased and harmful. Therefore, instruction ﬁne-tuned LLMs are
the recommended LLMs to use in speciﬁc AI applications for healthcare and medicine [ 1].

Since its release by the US company OpenAI in November 2022, a chatbot, ChatGPT ,

3.6. Ethical and Regulatory Consideration for Generative AI and LLMs
The current mainstream view of the healthcare and medicine community towards
LLM is a caution to balancing regulatory and technical challenges as the generative AI
technology is still in the early experimental stage. For example, the well-known ChatGPT
model is ﬁne-tuned on Internet data instead of healthcare data. As the model output
is impacted by the training dataset, the experts do not recommend direct utilization of
ChatGPT without further specialization in healthcare or medicine [ 40]. It is well known that
LLMs can generate outputs that are untruthful, toxic, hallucinated, or simply not helpful to
the users [ 48]. Conversely , healthcare and medicine are safety-critical, “high stake” ﬁelds
that simply cannot afford negative consequences [ 35]. Therefore, adequate attention needs
to be paid to the following concerns with AI ethics: patient privacy and data security issues,
bias in AI algorithms, and implications of AI-generated content in healthcare and medicine.

3.5.1. Creating Synthetic Patient Health Records to Improve Downstream Clinical
T ext Mining
T o date, many LLMs, e.g., ChatGPT , are only available through their APIs [ 14]. This
raises privacy concerns for directly uploading patients’ data to LLM API for data mining.
T o tackle this challenge, T ang et al. propose a new training paradigm that ﬁrst uses a small
number of human-labeled examples for zero-shot learning via prompting on ChatGPT to
generate a large volume of high-quality synthetic data with labels [ 14]. Using these synthetic
data, they ﬁne-tuned a local model for the downstream task of biological named entity
recognition and relation extraction using three public data sets: BCBI Disease, BC5CDR
Disease, and BC5CDR Chemical. Their training paradigm provides a useful application of
LLMs to clinical text mining with privacy protection. It not only signiﬁcantly reduces time
and effort for data collection and labeling, but also simultaneously mitigates health data
privacy concerns.

Natural language generation includes two major types of tasks: (1) converting input
texts into new symbol sequences, such as text summarization and machine translation,
and (2) “open-ended” generation, which aims to generate new text or symbols in response
to the input prompt, e.g., question answering, crafting emails, composing news articles,
and writing computer codes [ 1]. This capability is useful for many tasks in healthcare and
medicine.
Knowledge-intensive NLP tasks refer to tasks that require a substantial amount of
background knowledge, whether it be speciﬁc knowledge in a particular domain, general
real-world knowledge, or expertise gained over time [ 1]. These tasks not only require
pattern recognition or syntax analysis but are also highly dependent on the memorization
and proper utilization of knowledge about speciﬁc entities, events, and common sense of the

3.1.2. Data
The impact of data on the models’ effectiveness starts from pre-training data and
continues through to the training, test, and inference data [ 6]. The quality , quantity , and
diversity of pre-training data signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the performance of LLMs [ 1]. Therefore,
pre-training base models on data from a speciﬁc healthcare or medical ﬁeld to produce
instruction ﬁne-tuned models are the recommended development method for downstream
machine learning tasks for these ﬁelds [ 13]. Of course, with abundant annotated data,
both base LLM and instruction ﬁne-tuned models can achieve satisfactory performance
on a particular task and meet the important privacy constraint for healthcare and medical
data [ 14].

3.7. Future Research and Development Directions
3.7.1. Establishing Legislation, Policy , and Framework of Responsible AI

LLMs must strive to augment their models by maintaining continuous human engagement
through the phases of system design, training, testing, and implementation [ 59]. This
approach would ensure human oversight or co-piloting to optimize the technology’s
efﬁcacy , coupled with a forward-looking stance to remedy the existing limitations and
further advance AI application within healthcare.
3.7.4. Developing New Methods to Prevent Hallucination
The efﬁcacy of the common LLMs, including T ext-Davinci, GPT-3.5, Llama 2, MPT , and
Falcon, fell short in a well-designed hallucination assessment [ 18]. Umapathi et al. found
that these LLMs were too sensitive to prompt framing and decoding parameters. Even
minor alterations in these parameters led to models that had previously produced accurate
responses to start hallucinating with erroneous outputs. This phenomenon suggests a
critical need for further research to improve the robustness of LLMs across diverse settings.
Therefore, developing new methods to prevent hallucinations in model outputs is vital
in ensuring the responsible use of AI within the safety-critical domains of healthcare and
medicine.

3.2. Methods to T rain LLMs
3.2.1. Fine-T uning LLMs
LLMs can be ﬁne-tuned by various strategies, e.g., modifying the number of param-
eters [ 18], size of the training data set, or the amount of computing used for training [ 1].
Fine-tuning LLMs will scale up the pretrained LLMs and signiﬁcantly improve their per-
formance in reasoning beyond the power-law rule to unlock unprecedented, fantastic
emergent abilities [ 6,19]. Emergent abilities refer to speciﬁc competencies that do not exist
in smaller models but become salient as the model scales. These include but are not limited
to nuanced concept understanding, sophisticated word manipulation, advanced logical

Chain-of-thought prompting imitates the human multi-step reasoning process in
problem-solving tasks. It enhances few-shot examples in the prompt with a series of
intermediate reasoning steps articulated in concise sentences that lead to the ﬁnal an-
swer [6,16,27]. This method can effectively draw out the reasoning capabilities of LLMs [ 27]
and shows substantial improvements in performance on math problem-solving tasks [ 28].
However , Singhal et al. did not ﬁnd signiﬁcant improvement in the performance of chain-
of-thought prompting over the few-shot prompting strategy when applied to medical
question-answering tasks [ 6].
Self-consistency prompting samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only
taking the greedy one [ 29]. Its logic is the common wisdom that a complex problem usually
has multiple reasoning paths to reach the correct solution. It then selects the most consistent
answer out of the sampled reasoning paths through unsupervised learning.

into two types [ 1]: (1) encoder–decoder or encoder-only language models and (2) decoder-

represented by the GPT family models, Pathways Language Model (PaLM) introduced by
Google [ 10], and LLaMA models from Meta, have and will continue to dominate the LLM
space because they are the foundation models for generative AI technologies.

3.7. Future Research and Development Directions
3.7.1. Establishing Legislation, Policy , and Framework of Responsible AI

LLMs must strive to augment their models by maintaining continuous human engagement
through the phases of system design, training, testing, and implementation [ 59]. This
approach would ensure human oversight or co-piloting to optimize the technology’s
efﬁcacy , coupled with a forward-looking stance to remedy the existing limitations and
further advance AI application within healthcare.
3.7.4. Developing New Methods to Prevent Hallucination
The efﬁcacy of the common LLMs, including T ext-Davinci, GPT-3.5, Llama 2, MPT , and
Falcon, fell short in a well-designed hallucination assessment [ 18]. Umapathi et al. found
that these LLMs were too sensitive to prompt framing and decoding parameters. Even
minor alterations in these parameters led to models that had previously produced accurate
responses to start hallucinating with erroneous outputs. This phenomenon suggests a
critical need for further research to improve the robustness of LLMs across diverse settings.
Therefore, developing new methods to prevent hallucinations in model outputs is vital
in ensuring the responsible use of AI within the safety-critical domains of healthcare and
medicine.

3.7.5. Developing New Evaluation Methods
The inherent breadth, complexity , and high stakes of healthcare and medicine necessi-
tate the ongoing development of resilient evaluation methodologies and frameworks to
assure LLM alignment within these speciﬁc domains [ 16]. This endeavor calls for interdisci-
plinary collaboration among AI researchers, clinicians, consumers, social scientists, ethicists,
and policymakers. The application of various scientiﬁc and sociocultural viewpoints is
essential to address the social and contextual ramiﬁcations, thereby ensuring equitable and
responsible AI innovation [ 6].
A notable challenge associated with the use of similarity metric scores, such as
BERTScores, to evaluate LLM outputs lies in a narrow focus on the resemblance to a
golden standard (e.g., physician’s response), rather than assessing the accuracy or applica-
bility of the generated content [ 32]. The process of human analysis, although critical, can

pattern recognition or syntax analysis but are also highly dependent on the memorization
and proper utilization of knowledge about speciﬁc entities, events, and common sense of the
real world. Healthcare and medicine tasks ﬁt into this category . After exposure to a billion
tokens, LLMs are excellent at knowledge-intensive tasks. However , in situations where
LLMs have not learned the contextual knowledge or face tasks requiring this knowledge,
LLMs would struggle and might “hallucinate” [ 11]. This problem can be solved by further
exposing the LLM to the speciﬁc healthcare and medical knowledge base for retrieval
augmentation to develop instruction ﬁne-tuned models [ 15].

One paper classiﬁed under Level 2 explored ChatGPT’s utility as a support tool
on breast tumor board decision making [ 38]. In this study , the researchers provided
ChatGPT-3.5 with clinical information of ten consecutive patients presented in the breast
tumor board of a medical center in Israel. Then, they asked the chatbot to conduct three
tasks: summarization, recommendation, and explanation. Interestingly , the chatbot’s
recommendations were congruent with the tumor board’s decisions in 70% of the cases.
However , the chatbot did not recommend the inclusion of a radiologist in multidisciplinary
consultations.

3.5.1. Creating Synthetic Patient Health Records to Improve Downstream Clinical
T ext Mining
T o date, many LLMs, e.g., ChatGPT , are only available through their APIs [ 14]. This
raises privacy concerns for directly uploading patients’ data to LLM API for data mining.
T o tackle this challenge, T ang et al. propose a new training paradigm that ﬁrst uses a small
number of human-labeled examples for zero-shot learning via prompting on ChatGPT to
generate a large volume of high-quality synthetic data with labels [ 14]. Using these synthetic
data, they ﬁne-tuned a local model for the downstream task of biological named entity
recognition and relation extraction using three public data sets: BCBI Disease, BC5CDR
Disease, and BC5CDR Chemical. Their training paradigm provides a useful application of
LLMs to clinical text mining with privacy protection. It not only signiﬁcantly reduces time
and effort for data collection and labeling, but also simultaneously mitigates health data
privacy concerns.

On the other hand, based on the training data set, LLMs are classiﬁed into foundation
(or base) LLMs [ 11] and instruction ﬁne-tuned LLMs [ 1]. The foundation LLMs, e.g.,
ChatGPT , are trained to predict the next most likely word that will follow based on the text
training data; thus, the direction of output can be unpredictable. An instruction ﬁne-tuned
LLM is a base LLM to be ﬁne-tuned, using various techniques, including Reinforcement
Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [ 12]. As the instruction ﬁne-tuned LLMs are better
tuned to understand the context, input, and output in a speciﬁc application domain, they
have improved their ability to align with purpose, overcoming the limitations in the base
model, being safe and less biased and harmful. Therefore, instruction ﬁne-tuned LLMs are
the recommended LLMs to use in speciﬁc AI applications for healthcare and medicine [ 1].
This is supported by the ﬁnding of Singhal et al. that the instruction ﬁne-tuned Flan-PaLM
model surpassed its base PaLM model on multiple-choice medical question answering [ 6].

There are three key factors in choosing LLMs to solve practical problems: models, data,
and downstream tasks [ 1], which also apply to solve healthcare and medicine problems.
3.1.1. Models
Based on model training strategies, architectures, and use cases, LLMs are classiﬁed
into two types [ 1]: (1) encoder–decoder or encoder-only language models and (2) decoder-
only models. The encoder-only models represented by BERT family models have started
to phase out after the debut of ChatGPT . Encoder–decoder models, e.g., Meta’s BART ,
remain promising as most of them are open-sourced, providing opportunities for the
global software community to continuously explore and develop. Decoder-only models,
represented by the GPT family models, Pathways Language Model (PaLM) introduced by
Google [ 10], and LLaMA models from Meta, have and will continue to dominate the LLM
space because they are the foundation models for generative AI technologies.
On the other hand, based on the training data set, LLMs are classiﬁed into foundation
(or base) LLMs [ 11] and instruction ﬁne-tuned LLMs [ 1]. The foundation LLMs, e.g.,

RLHF refers to methods that combine three interconnected model training processes:
feedback collection, reward modeling, and policy optimization [ 22]. RLHF has been imple-
mented as instruction prompts to train LLMs to achieve remarkable performance across
many NLP tasks [
6,16,18]. It not only improves model accuracy , factuality , consistency ,
and safety and mitigates harm and bias within medical question-answering tasks [ 6], but
also bridges the gap between LLM-generated answers and human responses. Therefore,
RLHF brings LLMs considerably closer to practical applications within real-world clinical
settings.

Prompt engineering reﬁnes prompts for generative AI to generate text or images,
often through an iterative reﬁnement process. T o date, ﬁve instruction prompts have been
reported: zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, self-consistency , and ensemble reﬁnement
learning.

prompt instructions, eliminating the need for annotated data [ 23]; e.g., people enter in-

can contribute enormously to the prosperity , equality , and security of all’ [ 2].

3.7. Future Research and Development Directions
3.7.1. Establishing Legislation, Policy , and Framework of Responsible AI

There are three key factors in choosing LLMs to solve practical problems: models, data,
and downstream tasks [ 1], which also apply to solve healthcare and medicine problems.
3.1.1. Models
Based on model training strategies, architectures, and use cases, LLMs are classiﬁed
into two types [ 1]: (1) encoder–decoder or encoder-only language models and (2) decoder-
only models. The encoder-only models represented by BERT family models have started
to phase out after the debut of ChatGPT . Encoder–decoder models, e.g., Meta’s BART ,
remain promising as most of them are open-sourced, providing opportunities for the
global software community to continuously explore and develop. Decoder-only models,
represented by the GPT family models, Pathways Language Model (PaLM) introduced by
Google [ 10], and LLaMA models from Meta, have and will continue to dominate the LLM
space because they are the foundation models for generative AI technologies.

per_question.question: How do foundation LLMs differ from instruction fine-tuned LLMs, and what data strategy is recommended for healthcare?
per_question.response:
**Difference**  
- **Foundation (base) LLMs** are trained only to predict the next word from large, general‑domain text, so their outputs can be unpredictable and they are not specifically aligned to a task.  
- **Instruction‑fine‑tuned LLMs** start from a base model and are further fine‑tuned (e.g., with RLHF) to follow instructions, understand context, and produce safer, less biased answers that are better aligned with a specific application such as healthcare [1].

**Recommended data strategy for healthcare**  
- Pre‑train a base model on data drawn from the specific healthcare or medical field, then create instruction‑fine‑tuned models on that domain‑specific data. With sufficient annotated data, both base and fine‑tuned models can perform well while meeting privacy constraints [3].

and downstream tasks [ 1], which also apply to solve healthcare and medicine problems.
3.1.1. Models
Based on model training strategies, architectures, and use cases, LLMs are classiﬁed
into two types [ 1]: (1) encoder–decoder or encoder-only language models and (2) decoder-
only models. The encoder-only models represented by BERT family models have started
to phase out after the debut of ChatGPT . Encoder–decoder models, e.g., Meta’s BART ,
remain promising as most of them are open-sourced, providing opportunities for the
global software community to continuously explore and develop. Decoder-only models,
represented by the GPT family models, Pathways Language Model (PaLM) introduced by
Google [ 10], and LLaMA models from Meta, have and will continue to dominate the LLM
space because they are the foundation models for generative AI technologies.

per_question.question: Compare zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting and what the paper says about their results in medical question answering.
per_question.response:
**Zero‑shot prompting**  
* Uses a single instruction prompt with no example inputs.  
* Eliminates the need for annotated data and avoids catastrophic forgetting because the model parameters are not updated [2][4].  
* The paper does not give a specific performance figure for medical‑question answering, but notes that zero‑shot learning has been shown effective for a range of natural‑language‑understanding tasks [2].

**Few‑shot prompting**  
* Supplies a small set of input–output examples (typically a few) together with the task description.  
* Enables faster in‑context learning and yields more generalized, task‑specific performance than zero‑shot [2].  
* In experiments on hallucination control, performance improvements plateaued after three examples, and the authors stress that concise, explicit prompts are crucial for higher task‑execution accuracy [2].

**Chain‑of‑thought (CoT) prompting**  
* Extends few‑shot prompting by asking the model to generate a series of intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer.  
* Has shown large gains on math problem‑solving tasks [1], but **did not produce a significant improvement over standard few‑shot prompting for medical question‑answering** (Singhal et al.) [1].

**Overall comparison in the medical QA context**  
* Zero‑shot is mentioned as a viable approach but without reported medical‑QA results.  
* Few‑shot improves performance up to about three examples, with prompt clarity being key.  
* Chain‑of‑thought, despite its success in other domains, was not found to outperform few‑shot prompting on medical QA tasks. [1][2]

per_question.question: What evidence does the paper give that LLMs can help with patient communication?
per_question.response:
The paper cites several empirical studies showing that large‑language models can enhance communication with patients:

* In a cross‑sectional study of 195 Reddit patient questions, clinicians rated ChatGPT’s replies higher than physicians’ in 78.6 % of the 585 evaluations, noting significantly greater quality and empathy. The authors conclude that, with physician review, AI chatbots can help draft patient‑facing responses【1】.  
* Another evaluation found that both the CLAIR‑Long system and ChatGPT scored well on responsiveness, empathy and accuracy (though usefulness was neutral), leading the authors to state that LLMs have “significant potential for improving communication between patients and primary‑care providers”【3】.  

These findings provide direct evidence that LLM‑based chatbots can produce empathetic, high‑quality answers and thus support patient communication.

per_question.question: Which ethical and safety concerns does the paper raise about using generative AI in healthcare?
per_question.response:
The paper warns that using generative AI and large‑language models in health care raises a range of ethical and safety issues, including:

* **Patient privacy and data‑security risks** – prompts sent to services such as ChatGPT are transferred to the provider’s servers without legal safeguards and may violate data‑privacy laws [6].  
* **Bias and fairness problems** – training data and algorithmic choices can reproduce existing health inequities and cultural bias (e.g., English‑centric bias in Instruct‑GPT) [3][5].  
* **Untruthful, toxic or hallucinated outputs** – LLMs can generate false, offensive, or irrelevant information that could harm patients or clinicians [2][5][7].  
* **Accountability, transparency and explainability gaps** – the current evaluation frameworks are subjective and lack comprehensive coverage, making it hard to hold systems accountable or understand their decisions [5].  
* **Value‑alignment and purpose concerns** – AI‑generated content must be aligned with ethical norms, values and the intended purpose of health‑care delivery [5].  
* **Overall safety‑critical stakes** – because health care is a high‑risk domain, any negative consequences from erroneous AI output are unacceptable [2].

These concerns together form the ethical and safety challenges the paper highlights for generative AI in health‑care.

The current mainstream view of the healthcare and medicine community towards
LLM is a caution to balancing regulatory and technical challenges as the generative AI
technology is still in the early experimental stage. For example, the well-known ChatGPT
model is ﬁne-tuned on Internet data instead of healthcare data. As the model output
is impacted by the training dataset, the experts do not recommend direct utilization of
ChatGPT without further specialization in healthcare or medicine [ 40]. It is well known that
LLMs can generate outputs that are untruthful, toxic, hallucinated, or simply not helpful to
the users [ 48]. Conversely , healthcare and medicine are safety-critical, “high stake” ﬁelds
that simply cannot afford negative consequences [ 35]. Therefore, adequate attention needs
to be paid to the following concerns with AI ethics: patient privacy and data security issues,
bias in AI algorithms, and implications of AI-generated content in healthcare and medicine.

The large-scale use of ChatGPT has raised several social and ethical questions, e.g.,

data privacy legislations in many countries. Safeguarding AI systems and data is another
critical concern for generative AI application in healthcare and medicine, which requires
adequate data protection mechanisms to prevent unauthorized access as well as protection
against adversarial cyber-attacks [ 52]. These concerns prohibit the direct use of commercial
products, e.g., ChatGPT , in healthcare and medicine practice. They drive the research on
the alignment of generative AI and LLMs with appropriate norms, values, and design
goals [ 53].
3.6.3. Addressing Biases in AI Algorithms
It is well-recognized that foundation LLMs can generate outputs that are untruthful,
biased, toxic, hallucinated, or simply not helpful to users [ 48]. This is because the training
objective is to predict the next token in a text instead of following the user ’s instructions
helpfully and safely [ 26]. For example, the OpenAI company recognizes that their Instruct-
GPT model is biased towards the cultural values of English-speaking people as it is trained
to follow instructions in English [ 48].

3.6.4. Implications of AI Model “Hallucination” for Healthcare
An obvious limitation of LLMs is hallucination, which refers to the LLMs’ potential
to generate information that, though plausible, may be unveriﬁed, incorrect, or false [ 48].
This impediment can cause serious consequences in healthcare applications [ 18], leading to
inappropriate medical decisions that may compromise patient safety [ 38]. The fault may
further have profound legal and liability ramiﬁcations.

Based on model training strategies, architectures, and use cases, LLMs are classiﬁed
into two types [ 1]: (1) encoder–decoder or encoder-only language models and (2) decoder-
only models. The encoder-only models represented by BERT family models have started
to phase out after the debut of ChatGPT . Encoder–decoder models, e.g., Meta’s BART ,
remain promising as most of them are open-sourced, providing opportunities for the
global software community to continuously explore and develop. Decoder-only models,
represented by the GPT family models, Pathways Language Model (PaLM) introduced by
Google [ 10], and LLaMA models from Meta, have and will continue to dominate the LLM
space because they are the foundation models for generative AI technologies.

per_question.question: Compare the US and UK approaches to AI regulation described in the paper.
per_question.response:
**U.S. approach**

* The Biden‑Harris Administration plans to codify AI‑responsibility principles through an executive order and bipartisan legislation, positioning the United States as a leader in “responsible innovation” [1].  
* The White House has built a voluntary commitment process with the country’s largest AI firms, focusing on three core principles—safety, security and trust—and is working on an international framework to govern AI creation and use [5].

**U.K. approach**

* The U.K. government is running a public‑consultation that proposes five non‑statutory AI principles: (1) safety, security and robustness; (2) transparency and explainability; (3) fairness; (4) accountability and governance; and (5) contestability and redress [1].  
* These principles will be applied by existing regulators, with an emphasis on a pragmatic, proportionate, agile and iterative implementation that tailors rules to the specific context of AI deployment [2].

**Comparison**

* The U.S. strategy leans on formal executive and legislative actions plus voluntary industry pledges, aiming for a broad, internationally‑aligned framework.  
* The U.K. strategy relies on a consultative, non‑statutory set of principles administered by current regulators, emphasizing flexibility and proportionate oversight.

per_question.question: What evaluation methods and frameworks have been used to assess LLM answers in medicine?
per_question.response:
Several human‑centric evaluation approaches and structured frameworks have been applied to judge LLM outputs in medical contexts:

* **Human pairwise‑ranking** of model versus physician answers on a set of clinically‑relevant axes, combined with **physician assessment on adversarial test sets** designed to probe LLM limits【2†L2-L5】.  
* **Criterion‑based scoring** such as the **accuracy‑concordance‑insight (ACI)** triad used to compare ChatGPT with physicians【2†L6-L9】, and the four‑criterion set (empathy, responsiveness, accuracy, usefulness) employed for CLAIR‑Long, ChatGPT, and primary‑care physicians【2†L10-L13】.  
* **Singhal et al.’s multi‑axis frameworks**: an initial **seven‑axis rubric** (agreement with scientific/clinical consensus; reading comprehension/retrieval/reasoning; missing/incorrect content; potential harm; demographic bias; lay‑user helpfulness; intent coverage) for physician and lay‑user evaluation【4†L9-L13】, later expanded with **pairwise ranking on nine axes** and additional adversarial evaluations【4†L14-L16】.  
* **Simplified versions of the above** (seven questions across three axes: intent & helpfulness, clinical harm, clinical appropriateness) used to assess ChatGPT’s zero‑shot responses to postoperative cataract patients【7†L2-L5】.  
* Calls for **holistic, multi‑turn dialogue and active‑information‑procurement frameworks**, as well as rigorous rubrics to reduce labor‑intensity and inter‑rater variability【3†L2-L5】【3†L6-L9】.  

Together, these methods combine quantitative criteria, pairwise comparisons, adversarial testing, and comprehensive multi‑axis rubrics to evaluate LLM performance, fairness, bias, and safety in medicine.

per_question.question: What does the paper say about LLMs supporting clinical decision-making?
per_question.response:
The paper reports that large language models have demonstrated the ability to aid clinical decision‑making. In tests using 36 published clinical vignettes, ChatGPT achieved an overall 71.7 % accuracy (60.3 % for initial differential diagnoses and 76.9 % for final diagnoses), providing evidence to endorse their integration into the clinical workflow and to support decision‑making throughout the care process【1†L1-L4】【2†L5-L9】.  

Other models such as Med‑PaLM 2 and GPT‑4 have also shown high accuracy on medical‑exam questions (86.5 % and 86.1 % respectively) and were preferred by physicians for clinical utility, suggesting they can produce trustworthy, explainable outputs that could be incorporated into decision‑making and medical education【3†L1-L6】.  

Additionally, the paper notes that LLMs can improve interpretability, reduce documentation burden, and thereby enhance safety, quality, and efficiency in healthcare, further supporting their role in clinical decision‑support【4†L7-L13】.

per_question.question: What future research and development directions does the paper recommend?
per_question.response:
The paper outlines several priority areas for future research and development:

* **Establishing legislation, policy, and a responsible‑AI framework** – governments should create robust, safety‑focused regulations and international agreements for generative AI [1].

* **Maintaining continuous human involvement** – LLM development should embed human oversight throughout design, training, testing and deployment to improve efficacy and address current limitations [2].

* **Developing methods to prevent hallucinations** – new techniques are needed to make model outputs more robust and avoid erroneous, hallucinated answers, especially in safety‑critical health settings [1][5].

* **Creating new evaluation methodologies** – resilient, interdisciplinary evaluation frameworks are required that go beyond simple similarity metrics and assess accuracy, applicability, and equity of LLM outputs in healthcare [5][6].

* **Promoting interdisciplinary, human‑centered alignment** – collaborative roadmaps that align AI with human values, intents, and abilities across diverse domains and cultural contexts should be pursued [3][4].

These directions collectively aim to ensure AI systems are safe, trustworthy, ethically aligned, and effective for healthcare and other high‑stakes applications.

per_question.question: What did the Med-HALT study conclude about hallucination, and which models did best?
per_question.response:
The Med‑HAL T evaluation showed that hallucination is still a pervasive problem for current LLMs—none of the models achieved an “acceptable” level of accuracy on the hallucination tasks [2]. Nevertheless, the study identified two models that consistently outperformed the others:

* **Llama 2 (70 B)** – achieved the highest accuracy (42.21 %) and the best point‑wise score (52.37) on the false‑confidence reasoning test [1].
* **Falcon (40 B)** – excelled on the reasoning‑fake test, reaching 99.89 % accuracy (score 18.56) and showing the strongest ability to distinguish real from fabricated questions [1].

Overall, Llama 2 and Falcon outperformed commercial variants such as GPT‑3.5 and Text‑Davinci across all hallucination tasks, but even the best performers fell short of a satisfactory accuracy threshold [2].

At the same time, the authors note that pursuing alignment often entails an **“alignment tax”**—a trade‑off in which improving alignment (e.g., making outputs more helpful, honest, and ethical) can come at the cost of reduced performance on certain tasks [1].

per_question.question: Why can't hospitals just plug ChatGPT straight into clinical practice?
per_question.response: Hospitals can’t simply install ChatGPT in patient‑care settings because the technology raises several regulatory, safety and performance issues.  Current data‑privacy laws and the need to protect AI systems from unauthorized access or cyber‑attacks mean that commercial products such as ChatGPT are not permitted for direct clinical use without additional safeguards and alignment with legal norms [5].  Moreover, the model can produce untruthful, biased or “hallucinated” answers and often struggles with complex, procedural or critical‑thinking questions that are essential in clinical decision‑making [6].  Consequently, ethical, legal and safety guidelines require a careful, collaborative design and validation process before such generative AI can be deployed in healthcare [3].

Since its release by the US company OpenAI in November 2022, a chatbot, ChatGPT ,

people work, learn, travel, get health care, and communicate with each other ’, bringing in
signiﬁcant productivity improvement and reducing some of the world’s worst inequities,
particularly for health [ 1]. The White House media release acclaimed that ‘From cancer
prevention to mitigating climate change to so much in between, AI—if properly managed—
can contribute enormously to the prosperity , equality , and security of all’ [ 2].

ogy . Generative AI refers to a subset of AI technologies that learn to predict the next word
or sequence of words giving the preceding context. They can generate new content, such as
text, images, music, speech, video, or code. Their huge success has attracted unprecedented
speed of adoption, excitement, and controversy . Generative AI models use advanced

The inherent breadth, complexity , and high stakes of healthcare and medicine necessi-

and policymakers. The application of various scientiﬁc and sociocultural viewpoints is
essential to address the social and contextual ramiﬁcations, thereby ensuring equitable and
responsible AI innovation [ 6].

3.6. Ethical and Regulatory Consideration for Generative AI and LLMs
The current mainstream view of the healthcare and medicine community towards
LLM is a caution to balancing regulatory and technical challenges as the generative AI
technology is still in the early experimental stage. For example, the well-known ChatGPT
model is ﬁne-tuned on Internet data instead of healthcare data. As the model output
is impacted by the training dataset, the experts do not recommend direct utilization of
ChatGPT without further specialization in healthcare or medicine [ 40]. It is well known that
LLMs can generate outputs that are untruthful, toxic, hallucinated, or simply not helpful to
the users [ 48]. Conversely , healthcare and medicine are safety-critical, “high stake” ﬁelds
that simply cannot afford negative consequences [ 35]. Therefore, adequate attention needs
to be paid to the following concerns with AI ethics: patient privacy and data security issues,
bias in AI algorithms, and implications of AI-generated content in healthcare and medicine.
3.6.1. Ethical Concerns
The large-scale use of ChatGPT has raised several social and ethical questions, e.g.,

data privacy legislations in many countries. Safeguarding AI systems and data is another
critical concern for generative AI application in healthcare and medicine, which requires
adequate data protection mechanisms to prevent unauthorized access as well as protection
against adversarial cyber-attacks [ 52]. These concerns prohibit the direct use of commercial
products, e.g., ChatGPT , in healthcare and medicine practice. They drive the research on
the alignment of generative AI and LLMs with appropriate norms, values, and design
goals [ 53].
3.6.3. Addressing Biases in AI Algorithms
It is well-recognized that foundation LLMs can generate outputs that are untruthful,
biased, toxic, hallucinated, or simply not helpful to users [ 48]. This is because the training
objective is to predict the next token in a text instead of following the user ’s instructions
helpfully and safely [ 26]. For example, the OpenAI company recognizes that their Instruct-
GPT model is biased towards the cultural values of English-speaking people as it is trained
to follow instructions in English [ 48].
